title: Light Signals, Transponders & Emergency Reporting

required_knowledge_points.title: ATC Light Gun Signals — The NORDO Backup System
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE WILL ask you to recite all light gun signals from memory — airborne AND on the ground. This is a memorization-mandatory item. The pilot who confuses 'Flashing Green' in flight (return for landing) with 'Steady Green' (cleared to land) has the wrong clearance.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: ATC light gun signals are a backup communication method used by tower controllers when an aircraft has a radio failure (NORDO). The light gun is a highly directional, focused beam aimed through a sight directly at a specific aircraft. SIGNAL MEANINGS — ON THE GROUND: Steady Green = Cleared for takeoff. Flashing Green = Cleared to taxi. Steady Red = Stop. Flashing Red = Taxi clear of runway in use. Flashing White = Return to starting point on airport. Alternating Red/Green = Exercise extreme caution. IN THE AIR: Steady Green = Cleared to land. Flashing Green = Return for landing (NOT a clearance to land — must receive Steady Green before touchdown). Steady Red = Give way to other aircraft and continue circling. Flashing Red = Airport unsafe, do not land. Flashing White = Not applicable in the air. Alternating Red/Green = Exercise extreme caution. ACKNOWLEDGING SIGNALS: during the day, rock the wings. At night, flash the landing light or navigation lights. The logic of the signals follows kinetic state: on the ground, 'Steady Red' means stop (halt kinetic energy). In the air, 'Steady Red' means continue circling (manage kinetic energy safely). 14 CFR 91.125 governs compliance with light signals.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### ATC Light Gun Signals — MEMORIZE THIS TABLE
| Signal | On the Ground | In the Air |
|---|---|---|
| **Steady Green** | Cleared for **takeoff** | Cleared to **land** |
| **Flashing Green** | Cleared to **taxi** | **Return** for landing (not cleared to land yet) |
| **Steady Red** | **Stop** | Give way, **continue circling** |
| **Flashing Red** | Taxi **clear of runway** | Airport **unsafe** — do not land |
| **Flashing White** | Return to **starting point** | Not applicable |
| **Alt. Red/Green** | Exercise **extreme caution** | Exercise **extreme caution** |

### Acknowledging Light Signals
- **Day:** Rock wings
- **Night:** Flash landing light or nav lights

### Key Distinction
- **Flashing Green in flight** = Return for landing ≠ cleared to land
- Must receive **Steady Green** before actually touching down

> ⚠️ **Checkride Trap:** The DPE will point to each signal and ask the meaning for both ground AND airborne. This is pure memorization — no room for error.

required_knowledge_points.title: Transponder Operations — Mode C, Squawk Codes, and ADS-B
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE asks: 'What are the emergency squawk codes?' and 'When must the transponder be on?' The pilot who leaves the transponder on Standby during taxi or who accidentally rolls through 7500 while changing codes has created a serious situation.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: A transponder allows ATC secondary surveillance radar to identify and track an aircraft's position and altitude. MODE C (ALT): transmits the aircraft's pressure altitude via a blind encoder to ATC. MODE S: transmits altitude plus a unique aircraft address code. ADS-B OUT: broadcasts GPS position, altitude, velocity, and aircraft identification continuously on 1090 MHz (Mode S transponder) or 978 MHz (UAT). WHEN TO USE: 14 CFR 91.215 requires that if the aircraft is equipped with an operable transponder, it must be ON and replying with altitude at ALL times — including during taxi. Modern ASDE-X surface radar uses transponder returns to track ground movements. STANDARD SQUAWK CODES: 1200 = VFR (normal operations). 7500 = Hijack. 7600 = Lost Communications. 7700 = Emergency. Mnemonic: 75 = taken alive (hijack), 76 = technical fix (comm failure), 77 = going to heaven (emergency). CODE ROLLING: when changing squawk codes on older mechanical transponders, the pilot may accidentally pass through 7500, 7600, or 7700. This triggers an alarm at the ATC facility. Best practice: switch to Standby while changing codes, then back to ALT. ADS-B LIMITATIONS: ADS-B only shows aircraft that are transmitting ADS-B Out. Many aircraft (gliders, experimentals, aircraft in Class G) may not have ADS-B — they are invisible on traffic displays but fully capable of causing a mid-air collision.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Transponder Modes
| Mode | What It Transmits | When Used |
|---|---|---|
| **Standby** | Nothing (warm but not replying) | Only while changing codes |
| **Mode C (ALT)** | Squawk code + pressure altitude | ✅ **ALL times** including taxi |
| **Mode S** | Code + altitude + unique aircraft ID | ✅ Same as Mode C |
| **ADS-B Out** | GPS position + velocity + ID | ✅ Required in most controlled airspace |

### Emergency Squawk Codes — MEMORIZE
| Code | Meaning | Mnemonic |
|---|---|---|
| **1200** | VFR normal | — |
| **7500** | Hijack | 75 = "taken alive" |
| **7600** | Lost comm | 76 = "technical fix" |
| **7700** | Emergency | 77 = "going to heaven" |

### Code Rolling Prevention
- Changing from 1200 → assigned code on mechanical dials may pass through 7500/7600/7700
- **Solution:** switch to STANDBY → change code → switch back to ALT

> ⚠️ **Checkride Trap:** 'When should your transponder be on?' Answer: **always** — including taxi. Standby on the ground is outdated practice; ASDE-X needs your transponder return.

required_knowledge_points.title: VFR Flight Following, NTSB Reporting, and Runway Status Lights
required_knowledge_points.why: Three knowledge areas the DPE tests together: 'What services does Flight Following provide?', 'When must you notify the NTSB?', and 'What are those red lights in the pavement?' Each has specific traps — Flight Following is advisory only, NTSB notification goes to the NTSB (not FAA), and RWSL lights extinguishing is NOT a clearance.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: VFR FLIGHT FOLLOWING (RADAR ASSISTANCE): a service provided by ATC on a workload-permitting basis. ATC provides traffic advisories ('Traffic, 11 o'clock, 5 miles, opposite direction'), safety alerts, and a discrete squawk code. The pilot requests by stating position, aircraft type, destination, and altitude. KEY LIMITATIONS: (1) Flight Following is advisory — pilot retains full see-and-avoid responsibility. (2) ATC can terminate service at any time due to workload. (3) Radar has blind spots at low altitudes and near terrain. (4) Not all aircraft appear on radar. NTSB REPORTING (49 CFR PART 830): the pilot must IMMEDIATELY notify the NTSB (not the FAA, not NASA ASRS) when an ACCIDENT occurs. An accident is defined as: death, serious injury, OR substantial damage. Substantial damage = damage that adversely affects structural strength, performance, or flight characteristics. EXCLUDED from substantial damage: ground damage to landing gear, wheels, tires, flaps, engine accessories, brakes, or wingtips. Certain INCIDENTS also require immediate notification: flight control malfunction, in-flight fire, overdue aircraft, and others listed in 830.5. RUNWAY STATUS LIGHTS (RWSL): a fully automated safety system using in-pavement red LEDs. Runway Entrance Lights (REL) protect taxiway-runway intersections. Takeoff Hold Lights (THL) protect aircraft on the runway. CRITICAL RULE: illuminated red lights = STOP, regardless of ATC clearance. Extinguished lights do NOT equal clearance — ATC verbal clearance is still required.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Flight Following — What You Get and Don't Get
| Service | Provided? |
|---|---|
| Traffic advisories (clock position, altitude, direction) | ✅ Yes |
| Safety alerts (terrain, obstructions) | ✅ Yes |
| Discrete squawk code | ✅ Yes |
| Navigation vectors | ❌ No — pilot navigates |
| Terrain clearance | ❌ No — pilot's responsibility |
| Weather avoidance | ❌ No — pilot's responsibility |
| Guaranteed coverage | ❌ No — workload permitting |

### NTSB Notification — When and Who
- **Report TO:** NTSB (NOT FAA, NOT NASA ASRS)
- **When:** IMMEDIATELY upon an **accident** or listed **incident**
- **Accident =** death, serious injury, OR substantial damage
- **Substantial damage =** affects structural strength, performance, flight characteristics
- **NOT substantial:** landing gear, wheels, tires, flaps, brakes, wingtip damage

### Runway Status Lights (RWSL)
| Component | Location | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **REL** (Runway Entrance Lights) | Taxiway-runway intersection | Warns: runway occupied/unsafe to enter |
| **THL** (Takeoff Hold Lights) | Runway centerline | Warns: runway not safe for takeoff |

- Red lights ON = **STOP** — overrides any prior ATC clearance
- Red lights OFF ≠ clearance — ATC verbal clearance still required

> ⚠️ **Checkride Trap:** 'Who do you report an accident to?' NTSB — not the FAA, not your insurance company, not NASA ASRS. Those serve different purposes.

required_knowledge_points.title: Declaring Emergencies — Authority, Resources, and the Paperwork Myth
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE asks: 'Under what circumstances should you declare an emergency?' The pilot who hesitates because they're afraid of paperwork may die because they delayed accessing ATC resources. 14 CFR 91.3(b) is the most powerful regulation in aviation — learn it.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: A pilot should declare an emergency IMMEDIATELY when in distress (serious/imminent danger requiring immediate assistance) or urgency (safety concern not requiring immediate assistance). THE POWER OF 91.3(b): 14 CFR 91.3(b) states that in an in-flight emergency requiring immediate action, the PIC may deviate from ANY rule of Part 91 to the extent required to meet the emergency. This is the broadest authority granted to any individual in the federal regulatory system. What an emergency declaration triggers: ATC clears airspace ahead of the aircraft, halts departures if needed, provides priority routing and vectors to the nearest suitable airport, and activates crash-fire-rescue (CFR) alerting. TERMINOLOGY: 'Mayday' (3 times) = distress. 'Pan-Pan' (3 times) = urgency. Plain-English declaration ('declaring an emergency') is equally valid and understood by all US ATC facilities. THE PAPERWORK MYTH: pilots frequently hesitate to declare because they believe it automatically triggers an FAA investigation or requires extensive paperwork. FACT: 14 CFR 91.3(c) states a written report is required ONLY IF requested by the Administrator. In practice, for legitimate emergencies (engine failure, electrical fire, medical emergency), the FAA rarely requests a report. The cost of hesitation (loss of altitude, fuel, options, or life) vastly exceeds the cost of a phone call from the FSDO.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### When to Declare
| Condition | Classification | Call |
|---|---|---|
| Serious/imminent danger, need immediate help | **Distress** | **Mayday, Mayday, Mayday** |
| Safety concern, not immediately life-threatening | **Urgency** | **Pan-Pan, Pan-Pan, Pan-Pan** |
| Any situation where doubt exists | **Declare** | *"Declaring an emergency"* (plain English) |

### What You Get When You Declare
- ✅ Airspace cleared ahead of your aircraft
- ✅ Priority routing and vectors to nearest airport
- ✅ Crash-fire-rescue (CFR) alerted and standing by
- ✅ Legal authority to deviate from ANY Part 91 rule (91.3(b))
- ✅ Other departures held if necessary

### The Paperwork Myth — BUSTED
- **Myth:** Declaring = automatic FAA investigation + mountain of paperwork
- **Fact:** 14 CFR 91.3(c) requires a report ONLY if the Administrator **requests** it
- **Reality:** For legitimate emergencies, the FAA rarely requests a report
- **The real cost:** Hesitating to declare while the situation degrades = **death**

> ⚠️ **Checkride Trap:** 'What authority does 91.3(b) give you in an emergency?' It lets you deviate from **ANY** rule in Part 91. It is the broadest authority in federal aviation regulation.

lesson_overview:
## Light Signals, Transponders, NTSB Reporting, and the Decision to Declare

This lesson covers the backup communication systems, surveillance technology, regulatory reporting requirements, and the most important single decision a pilot can make in an emergency.

**Light gun signals are aviation's last-resort communication system.** When every radio fails, a tower controller can still direct traffic using a focused beam of colored light aimed directly at a specific aircraft. The system is physically robust, immune to electromagnetic interference, and bridges the gap when technology fails. Every private pilot must have the complete signal table memorized: six signals, each with different meanings on the ground versus in the air. The most commonly confused pair is Flashing Green — on the ground it means cleared to taxi, but in the air it means return for landing, which is NOT a clearance to land. The pilot must wait for a subsequent Steady Green before touching down.

**The transponder transforms an aircraft from a raw radar blip into identified, altitude-reporting traffic.** Mode C provides the squawk code and pressure altitude to ATC's secondary radar. ADS-B Out adds GPS position, velocity, and identification, broadcasting continuously on 1090 or 978 MHz. The four emergency squawk codes must be memorized cold: 1200 for normal VFR, 7500 for hijack, 7600 for lost communications, 7700 for emergency. The transponder must be ON and replying with altitude at ALL times — including taxi, where modern surface radar depends on transponder returns to track ground movements.

**NTSB accident notification is immediate, mandatory, and goes to the NTSB — not the FAA.** The distinction between accident and incident, and between substantial damage and minor damage, determines the reporting obligation. Substantial damage means damage that adversely affects structural strength, performance, or flight characteristics. Ground damage to landing gear, wheels, tires, and wingtips is explicitly excluded. Reporting to the FAA's FSDO, filing a NASA ASRS report, or notifying your insurance company does NOT satisfy the 49 CFR Part 830 requirement.

**Runway Status Lights represent the newest layer of automated runway incursion protection.** The system uses in-pavement red LEDs driven by surface surveillance radar. When the algorithm detects a conflict, the lights illuminate instantly — faster than any controller can react. Red lights ON means STOP, regardless of what ATC just cleared you to do. The lights extinguishing does NOT constitute a clearance — ATC verbal authorization is still required.

**Declaring an emergency is not a sign of weakness — it is the single most powerful tool a pilot possesses.** 14 CFR 91.3(b) grants the pilot in command authority to deviate from ANY regulation to the extent required to meet an in-flight emergency. This triggers the full ATC resource matrix: cleared airspace, priority routing, crash-fire-rescue alerting. The persistent myth that declaring generates punitive FAA attention and mountains of paperwork has killed pilots who hesitated while their situation degraded. A written report is required only if the Administrator specifically requests one — and for legitimate emergencies, that request rarely comes.
